text.p: The mark rose in European late trading, helped by a slide in the lira after comments by a Bundesbank council member that Italy and Spain will not likely be among the first nations to join Europe's planned currency union, traders said.
Hans-Juergen Koebnick, Bundesbank council member, said on Wednesday Italy and Spain should be ready to join European monetary union by 2002 and not 1999.
"That is certainly why the lira has weakened significantly," said Francesco Giordano, chief economist at San Paolo Bank.
"It is definitely negative for Italy and the Italian currency," he added.
At 1638 GMT the lira was trading at 999.25/25 per mark, down from 992.75/3 in late Europe on Tuesday.
The peseta, however, was only down slighty and trading at 84.14/4 against the mark comapared to 84.07/4.10 in late Europe on Tuesday.

Earlier on Wednesday, comments made by Koebnick's colleague Reimut Jochimsen saying he saw risks of social unrest in France and other European countries due to accelerated government efforts towards integration also unsettled markets.
Consolidation in high-yielding bond markets, drifting off their heady highs, also spilled over into the lira, sterling and the peseta, traders said.
But activity remained focused on the positive outlook for the dollar and sterling markets despite a pullback of both currencies from fresh peaks on Tuesday.
In France, civil servants have called a broad-based 24-hour strike for Thursday in protest to government plans to trim their numbers by nearly 6,000 next year.
The move is seen as part of the wider drive to trim finances in order for the country to qualify for monetary union and a single European currency.

"There are still potential hurdles in the way of EMU, one of them being wether attitudes will change in some of the major economies - including France," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

Lyons said while the markets were concerned about the French franc, foreign holdings of French assets have already come down quite considerably. "Therefore, the franc is less exposed than it may previously have been," he added.
At 1550 GMT the mark was at 3.3833/36 francs against 3.3800/3405 in late European trade on Tuesday.
Aside from renewed scepticism over EMU, analysts and traders also noted comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer who said he was unable to tell if there was room for lower interest rates.

"Central rates have reached historically low levels. Naturally we do continue to observe very attentively the unfolding of the situation. And we do not start from the principle that we will have to raise rates in the near term," he said in an interview with daily Le Monde.
"Tietmeyer seems to be keeping his options open on rates," said Lyons.
"Basically, the Buba is keeping its options open on interest rates and I would not rule out another easing (of them)," he added.
